newsitem.title: USA: Clinton out to repeat first term's economic success.
newsitem.headline: Clinton out to repeat first term's economic success.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
President Bill Clinton plans to pursue the same economic policies in his second term that served him so well in the first -- cutting the budget deficit and promoting U.S. exports.
But administration officials admit it will be harder the second time around.
"We're going from the less difficult to the more difficult," White House chief economist Joseph Stiglitz told Reuters in an interview. "It gets harder and harder."
Democrat Clinton swept to victory over Republican Bob Dole on Tuesday, riding an upbeat economy to win four more years in the White House.

"We ought to be able to keep the economy going," Labour Secretary Robert Reich said, looking ahead to Clinton's second term. He told Reuters Financial Television he saw no reason why the 5-1/2-year-old economic expansion cannot continue for another four years.

Reich suggested the economy may be able to grow faster than the 2.3 percent annual rate the administration has forecast for 1997 and beyond, provided America perseveres with sound economic policies. Growth this year may top 2.5 percent.
Stiglitz said Clinton is determined to follow through on his pledge to balance the deficit-ridden federal budget by the year 2002. But the president does not intend to stop there.
"The real objective is not reducing the deficit to zero by 2002, but reducing the deficit permanently," Stiglitz, who heads Clinton's Council of Economic Advisers, said.
But that means tackling politically-popular entitlement spending by the government on the Social Security pension system and the Medicaid and Medicare health care programmes for the poor and elderly.
"Those programmes have done an enormous amount to alleviate poverty," Stigltiz said. "But they have to be put on a sound financial basis.

Clinton has said a joint effort between Democrats and Republicans -- perhaps a bilateral commission -- will be needed to address the surge in entitlement spending in the next century as the baby boom generation reaches retirement.
But it is not clear how Republican lawmakers -- who have been stung badly in this election by Democrat charges that they were out to bankrupt Medicare -- will respond.
On the trade front, Stiglitz said the administration wants to build on the host of market-opening initiatives it launched in Clinton's first term -- from North America to Asia.

But progress may not come as easily, as attention shifts from knocking down barriers to U.S. goods exports to taking on the subtle and complicated impediments abroad that hinder U.S. service companies such as telecommunications firms and banks.

So far, there is no sign the administration will try to use a weaker dollar to juice up exports -- a policy that it seemed to follow in Clinton's first two years in office before Robert Rubin took over as Treasury Secretary.

Rubin, whom administration insiders are betting will stay on in Clinton's second term, never tires of saying a strong dollar is in the U.S. interest, arguing that it keeps down U.S. inflation and interest rates.

But it also makes U.S. exports less competitive on world markets -- a point that U.S. car companies have made repeatedly to the administration, especially as regards the dollar's continued rise against the Japanese yen.
Rubin has turned a deaf ear to those complaints, although he has stressed the need for Japan to ensure domestic demand is strong, in part because that will boost its imports.

Many analysts believe Clinton stands a good chance of working with Congress to carry out a major part of his second-term economic agenda -- even though Republicans looked to have retained control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott from Missisippi said he and his fellow Republicans would work with Clinton to cut the budget deficit and taxes.
"We're going to work together and we're going to have smaller government and less taxes," Lott told supporters.

Stanley Collender, managing director at the Federal Budget Consulting Group of Burston-Marsteller, argued that a centrist coalition of Republicans and Democrats will ultimately hold the balance of power in Congress, not the parties themselves.
"The votes may be there for a centrist budget concentrating on spending cuts," Collender said, adding, "Clinton could actually be president when the budget is balanced."
But some other analysts were more pessimistic and saw political gridlock, rather than a breakthrough budget agreement, as the most likely outcome of the bitterly-fought election.
"Bipartisanship faces strong political headwinds," said Thomas Gallagher of Wall Street broker Lehman Brothers, adding, "Stalemate is at least as likely as bipartisanship."
